lesson.title: Let the Units Do the Work: Dimensional Analysis
lesson.summary: Dimensional analysis uses unit conversion factors, built from SI base units, as a self checking method for turning one quantity into another without guessing whether to multiply or divide.
lesson.body:
Dimensional analysis, also called the factor label method, is a problem solving strategy that treats units as algebraic quantities you can multiply, divide, and cancel just like numbers. It builds directly on SI Units, since chemistry relies on a small set of base units, meters for length, kilograms for mass, seconds for time, moles for amount of substance, and derived units built from them, and on Significant Figures, since a converted answer must still respect the precision of the original measurement. The core idea is simple: any quantity can be multiplied by a conversion factor, a fraction equal to 1 because its numerator and denominator represent the same physical amount, without changing the actual quantity, only the units it is expressed in.

A conversion factor comes from an equality between two units, such as 1 inch equals 2.54 centimeters, or 1000 milliliters equals 1 liter. Because both sides of that equality describe the same physical amount, the fraction 2.54 cm over 1 in, or its flip, 1 in over 2.54 cm, is equal to 1, and multiplying any quantity by 1 never changes its true value. The skill lies in choosing which version of the fraction to use, and dimensional analysis makes that choice almost automatic: you set up the fraction so the unit you want to cancel sits opposite where it appears in your starting quantity, leaving only the unit you want in the final answer.

Consider converting 3.5 kilometers to centimeters, a two step conversion. Starting with 3.5 km, multiply by the conversion factor 1000 m over 1 km, which cancels the km, leaving meters: 3.5 km x (1000 m / 1 km) = 3500 m. Then multiply by 100 cm over 1 m, which cancels the m, leaving centimeters: 3500 m x (100 cm / 1 m) = 350000 cm, or 3.5 x 10^5 cm in scientific notation. Notice that at every step, the unit being eliminated appears once in the numerator of the running quantity and once in the denominator of the conversion factor, so it cancels cleanly, and the only units left standing at the end are the ones you were asked for.

Chemistry problems often chain several conversion factors in a single setup, moving from one kind of unit to a completely different kind, such as converting a volume of gas into a number of molecules, or a mass of reactant into moles of product. The method works exactly the same way no matter how many factors are strung together: write the given quantity, then multiply by one conversion factor after another, canceling units as you go, until only the desired unit remains uncancelled. For example, finding how many seconds are in exactly 2.0 days uses two factors: 2.0 days x (24 h / 1 day) x (3600 s / 1 h) = 172800 s, which rounds to 1.7 x 10^5 s given that 2.0 days has two significant figures.

The real value of dimensional analysis is that it catches mistakes before you even finish the arithmetic. If you accidentally set up a conversion factor upside down, the units will not cancel properly, and you will be left with a nonsensical combination like cm times km instead of a clean single unit, which is an immediate signal that something in the setup is wrong. That built in error check is why this method remains the standard approach across chemistry, physics, and engineering for any problem that involves converting between units or combining several measured quantities into one final result.
